examples.name: Literal
examples.note: A string rule matches a literal; default matching is case-insensitive.

examples.name: Failure
examples.note: A literal that does not match returns false; the input and position are unchanged.

examples.name: Sequence and alternatives
examples.note: Default parsing skips intervening whitespace. Use [/all] to require exact spacing.

examples.name: Alternatives
examples.note: 0 separates ordered alternatives. The first successful branch wins.

examples.name: Repetition
examples.note: Encoded [ 1 rule ] means one or more; [ 2 rule ] means zero or more; [ 3 rule ] means optional.

examples.name: Recursive named rules
examples.note: Named rules live in a flat data registry. This rule is recursive.

examples.name: skip / to / thru / end
examples.note: [ 4 ] skips one byte, [ 5 target ] seeks without consuming, [ 6 target ] seeks and consumes, [ 7 ] matches end.

examples.name: to target
examples.note: to seeks to the target and leaves it unconsumed; the following literal consumes it.

examples.name: Character set
examples.note: A charset is [ 8 descriptor ]; descriptor is a byte string of lo,hi ranges. Sets are case-sensitive.

examples.name: copy capture
examples.note: copy records the source slice; capture names in this playground are strings so the host can display them.

examples.name: none and end
examples.note: 'none succeeds without consuming input. [ 7 ] matches end-of-input.
